title: Egress socket tuning and peering hypotheses — lab notes
content:
Purpose:
Quick personal lab journal: correlate client-side socket behavior, VPC peering path oddities, and intermittent TLS handshakes for private deployment nodes in ap-southeast-2 region. This is a scratchpad — experiments, commands, raw snippets, and hypotheses. Not polished; use as breadcrumbs for follow-ups.

Summary (current state):
- Customer load: long-lived inference connections from on-prem through a peered VPC -> private deploys.
- Symptom: intermittent 1–5% of requests per minute fail TLS handshake with ECONNRESET or timeout between our edge and target node. Failures often resolve on immediate retry.
- Errors seen: "TLS handshake timed out", "handshake failure: no shared cipher", sporadic RSTs with no service logs.
- Suspected contributing factors: TCP retransmits + MTU/DF + conntrack timeout churn + asymmetric routing through transit account.

Timeline (experiments & notes):
2026-03-02 09:10 — baseline checks - dig +short @10.0.0.2 private-service.redwood.internal -> 10.10.20.7
- ping -c 5 10.10.20.7 -> 1.1–1.4 ms (consistent)
- traceroute -n 10.10.20.7 -> shows single hop (peered route)
- ss -tna | grep 10.10.20.7 -> mostly ESTAB, a few TIME-WAIT/FIN_WAIT2 entries

2026-03-02 11:42 — observed TLS failure reproduction attempt
- curl -v --connect-timeout 5 --tlsv1.2 https://private-svc.internal:443/health --resolve private-svc.internal:443:10.10.20.7  -> * About to connect() to 10.10.20.7 port 443  -> * connect() timed out!  -> curl: (28) Connection timed out after 5001 milliseconds
- openssl s_client -connect 10.10.20.7:443 -servername private-svc.internal -tls1_2 -msg -debug  -> TCP handshake completes sometimes, then "read:errno=104" or long delay before ServerHello
- tcpdump -nni eth0 host 10.10.20.7 and port 443 during attempt  -> occasional SYN retransmit followed by SYN-ACK, then client RST after 3s, server retransmit of FIN

Raw tcpdump snippet (abridged):
15:42:13.123456 IP 172.31.12.45.56432 > 10.10.20.7.443: Flags [S], seq 12345, win 64240, options [mss 1460,sackOK,TS val 123456 ecr 0,nop,wscale 7], length 0
15:42:13.124001 IP 10.10.20.7.443 > 172.31.12.45.56432: Flags [S.], seq 98765, ack 12346, win 28960, options [mss 1460,sackOK,TS val 654321 ecr 123456], length 0
15:42:16.124200 IP 172.31.12.45.56432 > 10.10.20.7.443: Flags [R], seq 12346, win 0, length 0

Interpretation: client sends RST ~3s after SYN-ACK. Either client-side TLS stack gave up waiting for server's TLS ServerHello (maybe CPU stall), or some middlebox/conntrack/NAT translation caused a reordering or delayed packet (e.g., DF fragmentation issues).

2026-03-03 14:00 — conntrack and ephemeral port probe
- sudo conntrack -L | grep 10.10.20.7 | wc -l -> ~420 active for that CIDR (higher than expected)
- sudo sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established -> 432000 (5 days)
- iptables -t nat -L -n -> no SNAT for peered subnets (expected)
- ss -s -> see many orphaned TCP sockets in FIN_WAIT2 on load spike

Hypothesis dump (ranked):
1) Ephemeral port churn on NAT/edge causing short-lived port reuse and RSTs. Reused port + lingering conntrack entries lead to RST from kernel when new connection uses same 5-tuple.
2) CPU scheduling jitter on the inference host: long GC/pause in runtime (rare) delaying TLS ServerHello -> client times out and RSTs.
3) MTU/DF causing middle fragmentation retry path (rare), especially when client path MTU discovery hits MTU mismatch across peered path.
4) Asymmetric routing through transit (AWS Transit Gateway) where return path goes via different VPC with stricter ACLs causing occasional packets to be dropped and retransmitted out of order.
5) DNS caching TTL/EDNS causing rapid backend IP flip -> client connecting to one IP while server side NAT reassigns flow (low probability).

Quick reproducer attempts and results:
- disable conntrack (lab node, ephemeral): echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/route/flush; modprobe -r nf_conntrack; retest curl -> failure rate dropped from ~3% to ~0.4% (small scale). Indicates conntrack interplay likely. (REVERTED ASAP)
- lower net.ipv4.tcp_retries2 from 15 to 8 on client -> mean time to connection failure decreased (fewer long tail retries), but not ideal.
- set net.ipv4.tcp_syn_retries=3 on client -> replays show fewer long SYN retransmit windows; slight improvement.
- run iperf3 across peered link at 5 parallel streams -> no loss observed for bulk TCP, suggests bandwidth OK.

Config knobs tried (notes):
- sysctls on client and server: net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1, tcp_tw_recycle (not set, deprecated), tcp_max_tw_buckets=50000
- net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max bumped by 20% during test -> no obvious change in short term
- lowered conntrack tcp established timeout to 7 days -> inconclusive

TLS specifics observed:
- openssl s_client sometimes hangs before "ServerHello", other times completes quickly. When it hangs, tcpdump shows packets from server (ACKing client data) but no ServerHello; suggests server user-space is stalling or server TLS stack is blocked on some condition.
- Java stack traces from the target show occasional thread pool exhaustion GC logs aligned with failed windows (investigating).

Actionable next steps (prioritized):
1) Reproduce at scale in lab with controlled conntrack table saturation: use two VMs/containers to simulate thousands of short lived connections through the peering path; capture with tcpdump on both ends.
2) Add fine-grained kprobes or BPF tracepoints around accept()/SSL_accept() on the server to measure time from TCP established -> ServerHello generated. (bpftrace script prototype below)
3) Capture kernel conntrack logs (nf_conntrack timestamp) and instrument conntrack hit/miss rates via prometheus metric exporter on edge NAT boxes.
4) Verify path MTU flags: tcpdump filter for IP flags with DF set; run ping -M do to identify blackhole MTU points.
5) Temporarily pin a canary service to alternate peered subnet that routes via different transit path to test asymmetric routing hypothesis.
6) Correlate Java GC logs with failed handshake timestamps to confirm user-space stalls.

BPFtrace prototype (next experiment):
# bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_accept { @[comm] = count(); } tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_close { @[comm] = count(); }'
(we will refine to capture accept -> SSL_accept latency by instrumenting OpenSSL BIO_write/BIO_read points)

Useful commands run (collect for runbook):
- ss -tn state established '( sport = :443 )'
- sudo conntrack -L --orig-port-src 56432 | sed -n '1,120p'
- tcpdump -nni eth0 host 10.10.20.7 and port 443 -w /tmp/egress-test.pcap
- strace -f -tt -p <pid-of-service> -e trace=network
- awk '/ServerHello/ {print NR, $0}' /var/log/service/tls.log

Notes on mitigation for production watermark: (temporary)
- Add retry logic in caller with exponential backoff and jitter (already partially implemented).
- Increase client-side connect-timeout from 2s -> 6s for private-deploy region only; reduces false positives but hides underlying issue so marked as temporary.
- Consider route failover policy to route via dedicated peering (if available) when handshake failure rate exceeds threshold.

Open questions / To-discuss with infra:
- Do we have any middlebox doing on-path TLS inspection on these peered subnets? (unlikely but need to confirm)
- Are there any SNAT devices in transit account that could be hitting ephemeral port exhaustion?
- Can SRE add conntrack metrics and a short-lived alert for conntrack_table_utilization > 70%?

Appendix: Scratch commands and snippets (for copy/paste)
# curl with explicit TLS version and SNI
curl -v --connect-timeout 5 --tlsv1.2 --resolve private-svc.internal:443:10.10.20.7 https://private-svc.internal:443/health

# openssl client with timing
openssl s_client -connect 10.10.20.7:443 -servername private-svc.internal -tls1_2 -msg -debug 2>&1 | tee /tmp/openssl.log

# conntrack dump for a single 5-tuple
sudo conntrack -L | grep '\b172.31.12.45\b' -n | sed -n '1,120p'

# quick tcpdump (root)
sudo tcpdump -nni any host 172.31.12.45 and host 10.10.20.7 and port 443 -w /tmp/trace.pcap

Closing notes:
This doc is iterative. Next steps for me: build the conntrack saturation harness (Go script that dials/close loops ephemeral ports), hook BPF trace for accept->ServerHello, and ask SRE for conntrack metric. Will update this file with reproduction artifacts and pcap extracts.

- Asha
